source_text: Non dubito, frater, te post uxorem in pace praemissam, ad compositionem animi conversum, de exitu singularitatis cogitare, et utique consilii indigere. Quamquam in hujusmodi cum fide sua conloqui debet unusquisque, ejusque vires consulere; tamen quoniam, in ista specie, carnis necessitas cogitatum movet, quae fere apud eamdem conscientiam fidei resistit, opus est fidei extrinsecus consilio, tanquam advocato adversus carnis necessitates. Quae quidem necessitas facillime circumscribi potest, si voluntas potuis Dei, quam indulgentia consideratur. Nemo indulgentia utendo promeretur, sed voluntati obsequendo. Voluntas Dei est sanctificatio nostra. Vult enim imaginem suam nos etiam similitudinem fieri, ut simus sancti, sicuti ipse sanctus est. Id bonum, sanctificationem dico, in species distribuit complures, ut in aliqua earum deprehendamur. Prima species, virginitas a nativitate. Secunda virginitas, a secunda nativitate, id est a lavacro, quae aut in matrimonio purificat ex compacto, aut in viduitate perseverat ex arbitrio. Tertius gradus superest monogamia, cum post matrimonium unum interceptum exinde sexui renuntiatur. Prima virginitas felicitatis est, non nosse in totum a quo postea optabis liberari. Secunda virtutis est, contemnere cujus vim optime noris. Reliqua species hactenus nubendi post matrimonium morte disjunctum, praeter virtutis, etiam modestiae laus est. Modestia est enim, ablatum non desiderare, et ablatum a Domino Deo; sine cujus voluntate nec folium de arbore delabitur, nec passer assis unius ad terram cadit.
pass_a_gloss: I do not doubt, brother, that you, after your wife has been sent ahead in peace, have turned to the composing of your mind, and are thinking about the outcome of being single, and are certainly in need of counsel. Although each person ought to converse with his own faith about such things, and consult its powers, nevertheless, since in this kind of thing, the necessity of the flesh moves the thought, which almost always resists the same conscience of faith, external counsel of faith is needed, as if an advocate against the necessities of the flesh. This necessity can indeed be easily overcome, if the will of God is considered rather than indulgence. No one merits anything by using indulgence, but by obeying the will. The will of God is our sanctification. For He wants us to become His image and likeness, so that we may be holy, just as He is holy. This good, I say sanctification, is distributed into several kinds, so that we may be caught in one of them. The first kind is virginity from birth. The second virginity is from the second birth, that is, from the bath, which either purifies in marriage by compact, or perseveres in widowhood by choice. The third step remaining is monogamy, when after one marriage has been interrupted, renunciation of sex follows. The first virginity is a happiness, not to know at all what you will later wish to be freed from. The second is a virtue, to despise what you know the power of very well. The remaining kind, to marry after a marriage has been dissolved by death, is praise not only of virtue, but also of modesty. For modesty is not to desire what has been taken away, and what has been taken away by the Lord God, without whose will not a leaf falls from a tree, nor does a sparrow fall to the ground for a single coin.

pass_b_english: I do not doubt, brother, that after your wife went ahead of you in peace you have turned your mind to composing yourself and are now weighing what it means to stay single — and you certainly need counsel. True, everyone ought to hash this out with his own faith and test its strength; but because the flesh's necessity keeps prodding the thought, and that necessity almost always resists the very conscience of faith, you need faith's counsel from outside, like an advocate against the flesh's demands. That necessity is easily overcome if you weigh God's will instead of indulgence. No one earns anything by claiming indulgence; you earn by obeying the will. And God's will is our sanctification. He wants us to become his image and likeness so that we may be holy as he is holy. That good — sanctification, I mean — he parcels out into several forms so that we might be caught in one of them. The first form is virginity from birth. The second virginity comes from the second birth, that is, from baptism: it either keeps itself pure within marriage by mutual agreement, or it perseveres in widowhood by choice. The third step left is monogamy: after one marriage ends, you renounce sex altogether. The first virginity is happiness — never knowing at all the thing you will later long to be free of. The second is virtue — despising the power you know all too well. The remaining form, marrying again after death has dissolved a marriage, wins praise not only for virtue but also for modesty. For modesty means not craving what has been taken away, and taken away by the Lord God, without whose will not a leaf falls from a tree nor a sparrow drops to the ground for a single coin.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B both correctly handle the theological nuances and the list of virginity/monogamy stages. The scripture allusion (Matthew 10:29) is correctly rendered in both versions as 'not a leaf falls... nor does a sparrow fall...'.
